captions.text: Picture a farm, on a plain as flat as a table.
No hill, no lake.
At midday, the barn roof has sun to spare, and in the evening, the house is short of it.
How do you keep a little midday for tonight?
With a tower…
and a twenty-tonne weight.
What you lift, you can let back down.
Let’s follow one small ray of sunlight.
It lands on the roof, and now it is current.
It runs under the yard, to the foot of the tower.
Right at the top, it wakes a motor that spins very fast.
The gearbox turns that speed into force, and the drum reels in its rope, ever so gently.
Down there, twenty tonnes start to rise, at four metres a minute.
Our ray of sunlight has become height, and it waits up there, without wearing out.
In the evening, the weight comes down.
The motor becomes a generator, and the current comes back through the meter.
Back at the farm, where the house has been waiting.
That is the whole story: a ray of sunlight, twenty tonnes, twenty metres…
and one lit window.
Now for the figure that says it all.
One kilowatt-hour is one tonne raised three hundred and sixty-seven metres.
How wonderful: a little current, and a tonne goes higher than any cathedral!
And how disappointing: all that for one kettle, for half an hour.
Our tower holds one point zero nine kilowatt-hours.
And on a shelf in this room, a small box is waiting for you.
This battery module, forty kilos, holds as much as four point four towers.
Let’s say it plainly: at this scale, the battery wins.
That is not a defeat: that is where it gets interesting!
A few landmarks, for the investigation.
Four views: the farm, the tower, the hoist and the power room.
Click on a part: its sheet opens, and you can listen to its story.
The assembly guide tells how the tower goes up.
The installation guide goes from the yard to the power room.
The simulation lets you change the weight and the height, and run ten scenarios.
Six lessons, with quizzes, explain the physics.
The plans gather the drawings.
One last thing: this lab is an educational reconstruction.
The machine is generic, and nobody sells it.
The figures come from published sources or from our model.
The video I sometimes quote, a home builder in his courtyard, is in the Sources.
Over to you!

segments.title: A farm, a tower, one kilowatt-hour

captions.text: Welcome to the farm: a yard that is flat on purpose.
With no hill and no lake, there is no pumping water uphill here.
The barn roof gives up its midday surplus.
The current goes through the power shed, then dives into the trench, under the yard.
And the tower turns it into height: twenty tonnes, twenty metres.
In the evening, the house asks for it back.
The grid connection gives the current somewhere to go.
Around the tower, a fence keeps a wide circle empty, and its gate stops everything the moment it opens.
The mast, meanwhile, watches the wind across the plain.
And those copper-coloured blocks on the meadow?

In the shaft, two rails guide the load.

Four falls of rope hold the hook block, and they carry everything.

and the rope stays on its sheaves.
One serious word, just one.
Never stand under a suspended load.
And never build one without a structural engineer and a lifting inspector.
Even a home-sized version can kill.
